narrative:
The model predicted a 94% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the model toward a failure prediction. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of roughly the sixth and fifth deciles among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly outweighed other information.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in the opposite direction. At 3.10 it sat only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model a small reason for optimism.

Other details such as your LSAT score of 30 (versus an accepted-student average of 37), lower-middle family income, and full-time work plans played lesser roles and did not overcome the dominant negative signal from your law-school grades.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or enroll in a post-baccalaureate program, or consider retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger analytical skills. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
